reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: RAROC on a EUR 80m one-year loan. After-tax net income is already done: EUR 0.63m. The bank sets capital at risk as unexpected loss, $\alpha \times LGD \times EAD$, with $\alpha = 6\sigma$ and $\sigma = 2.0\%$ (standard deviation of historical default rates). $LGD = 40\%$, $PD = 1.0\%$. The regulator requires EUR 6.4m of capital for the loan.
ask: The RAROC denominator, capital at risk, is closest to:

options.label: ≈ EUR 6.4m
options.why: Used the regulatory capital requirement. The bank's own capital at risk is the unexpected loss $\alpha \times LGD \times EAD$, so the regulatory figure is a distractor.

options.label: ≈ EUR 9.6m
options.why: Applied $\alpha = 12\%$ to the whole exposure and forgot to multiply by LGD: $0.12 \times 80 = 9.6$.

takeaway: RAROC divides after-tax risk-adjusted income by the bank's own unexpected loss (here 12% of the 40% loss slice of EAD), not by the regulatory capital figure.

setup: Altman Z-score for a listed Canadian manufacturer (CAD m): total assets 600, total liabilities 390, book value of equity 210, market value of equity 330.
ask: In Altman's formula, $X_4$ (the equity-to-debt term) is closest to:

options.why: Used the book value of equity, $210/390$. Altman's $X_4$ is built on the MARKET value of equity.
Divided market equity by book equity, $330/210$, instead of by total liabilities.

takeaway: Altman's $X_4$ = market value of equity / total liabilities. The book equity figure in the table is a distractor.

setup: Altman $Z = 1.2X_1 + 1.4X_2 + 3.3X_3 + 0.6X_4 + 0.999X_5$, with $X_3 = \text{EBIT}/\text{total assets}$. A textile firm has total assets INR 400 crore and EBIT INR 170 crore. The other four terms are held fixed and add up to 1.7471, so $Z = 3.15$. The 'unlikely to default' zone is $Z > 3.0$.
ask: The largest EBIT fall that keeps the firm in the zone is closest to:

options.label: ≈ INR 0.045 crore
options.why: Stopped at the change in the ratio $X_3$ (0.0453) and never multiplied by total assets of 400.

options.label: ≈ INR 60 crore
options.why: Multiplied the 0.15 gap in Z by assets without dividing by the 3.3 weight on $X_3$.

options.label: ≈ INR 152 crore
options.why: Reported the EBIT level at which $Z = 3.0$ rather than the fall from 170 to that level.

takeaway: A Z-gap is turned into dollars by dividing by the term's weight and then multiplying by total assets. The 3.3 weight on EBIT makes small EBIT falls matter a lot.

setup: A rating agency's cumulative default rates for B-rated issuers are 7.40% by year 2 and 11.20% by year 3. Seen from today, the chance of defaulting during year 3 is $11.20 - 7.40 = 3.80\%$.
ask: The probability of defaulting in year 3 GIVEN survival through year 2, compared with 3.80%, is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Divided the wrong way. Conditioning on survival divides 3.80% by the survival rate (92.6%), which is below 1, so the figure grows.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Treated $C_3 - C_2$ as if it were already conditional. It is the unconditional view from time zero.

takeaway: Conditional PD = marginal PD / survival to the start of the year, so it always exceeds the unconditional figure once defaults have occurred.

setup: One-year rating migration matrix, years independent. Row X: 92% stay in X, 6% move to Y, 2% default. Row Y: 8% move to X, 82% stay in Y, 10% default. An issuer is rated X today.
ask: Its unconditional probability of default during year 2, compared with the 2% year-1 PD, is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Scaled 2% by the 98% that survive year 1 (1.96%), as if survivors kept the same 2% default rate. That ignores the 6% that migrate to Y.

options.label: Equal to 2%
options.why: Assumed a constant default rate. The matrix moves some issuers into Y, where default risk is five times higher.

working.label: Defaults from X after staying in X

takeaway: For good grades the marginal PD rises with time because migration feeds the riskier grades. Cumulative two-year PD is 4.44%.

setup: Merton model over a 3-year horizon, with the risk-free rate as asset drift: $d_2 = 1.60$, so the risk-neutral PD by year 3 is $N(-1.60) = 5.48\%$. The firm's expected asset return is 9%. A CVA system needs one constant average hazard rate.
ask: The hazard rate to enter, per year, is closest to:

options.why: Divided $-\ln(1-0.0548) = 0.0564$ by $T^2 = 9$ instead of by $T = 3$.
Entered the 3-year cumulative PD as if it were an annual rate.
Scale slip (10×). A 19% annual hazard would imply about 43% default within three years.

takeaway: Average hazard = $-\ln(1-Q(T))/T$. The 9% expected return would give a real-world PD, not the risk-neutral one a CVA system needs.

setup: A five-year CDS on a mining company trades at 180 bp, with expected recovery of 35%. The average hazard rate follows from $s = \bar\lambda\,(1-R)$.
ask: The implied average hazard rate, compared with the 1.80% spread, is:

options.label: Lower than 1.80%
options.why: Multiplied the spread by $(1-R)$ instead of dividing: $1.80\% \times 0.65 = 1.17\%$.

options.label: Equal to 1.80%
options.why: Ignored recovery, which is only valid when the loss given default is 100%.

takeaway: The spread pays for expected loss, $\lambda \times LGD$, so the hazard rate is always above the spread when recovery is positive.

setup: CDS spreads on one name, recovery 40%: 3-year 400 bp, 5-year 350 bp. The average hazard rate to each maturity is $s/(1-R)$, giving 6.67% to year 3 and 5.83% to year 5.
ask: The average hazard rate between year 3 and year 5 must be:

options.label: Between 5.83% and 6.67%
options.why: Averaged the two figures (6.25%). The 5-year number already contains the 3-year hazard, so the forward rate must lie on the far side of it.

options.label: Above 6.67%
options.why: Swapped the averages in the bootstrap, $(5 \times 6.67 - 3 \times 5.83)/2 = 7.9\%$.

takeaway: An average that falls as the horizon lengthens means the forward hazard is below the longer average. An inverted CDS curve signals near-term distress.

setup: Merton model, one year: asset value JPY 800bn, debt due 600bn, asset volatility 20%, risk-free rate 4%, expected asset return 10% (continuous). With the risk-free drift the distance to default is 1.54, a risk-neutral PD of 6.2%. A stress scenario needs the real-world PD.
ask: The real-world PD, compared with 6.2%, is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Read the higher expected return as extra risk. A higher drift pushes assets further above the debt, so distance to default widens and PD shrinks.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only the drift changes between the two cases, but the drift enters the numerator of the distance to default.

takeaway: Real-world PD uses the expected return $\mu$ as drift; risk-neutral uses $r$. When $\mu > r$ the real-world PD is the smaller one.

setup: Merton distance to default $d_2$, computed with the risk-free rate over the whole life of the debt. Borrower (KRW bn): assets 500, zero-coupon debt 300 due in 2 years, asset volatility 22%, risk-free rate 4%. Bands: DD 3.0 or more A; 2.0 to below 3.0 BBB; 1.0 to below 2.0 BB; below 1.0 B.
ask: The borrower's band is:

options.label: BBB
options.why: Used a one-year horizon (DD about 2.39). The debt runs for two years, so the numerator picks up two years of drift and the s.d. is $0.22\sqrt{2}$.

options.label: B
options.why: Kept only the drift term and dropped $\ln(A/D)$, which gives DD about 0.10.

takeaway: Use the debt's own maturity in both the drift term and $\sigma\sqrt{T}$. The one-year short form would flatter the borrower by a full band.

setup: Basel II IRB on a residential mortgage book: EAD GBP 400m, PD 1.50%, LGD 25%, average remaining maturity 18 years, 99.9% confidence. Retail correlation is fixed at 0.15, which gives a worst-case default rate (WCDR) of 14.56%. Capital is $K = EAD \times LGD \times (WCDR - PD)$.
ask: The risk-weighted assets are closest to:

options.label: ≈ GBP 13m
options.why: Stopped at the capital charge $K$ and never multiplied by 12.5 to convert it into RWA.

options.label: ≈ GBP 575m
options.why: Applied a corporate-style maturity adjustment (about 3.5 for 18 years). Retail exposures carry no maturity adjustment.

options.label: ≈ GBP 5,000m
options.why: Took RWA as $12.5 \times EAD$ and skipped the capital formula altogether.

takeaway: RWA = 12.5 × K. The 18-year maturity is a distractor for retail; the risk weight here is about 41% of EAD.

setup: Basel II advanced IRB, corporate loan of EUR 250m, $PD = 0.80\%$, $LGD = 40\%$, maturity $M = 4$ years. The maturity slope is $b = [0.11852 - 0.05478\ln(PD)]^2 = 0.1467$, and the maturity adjustment is $MA = \dfrac{1 + (M - 2.5)\,b}{1 - 1.5\,b}$.
ask: The multiplier $MA$ applied to capital is closest to:

options.why: Computed the numerator $1 + 1.5 \times 0.1467$ and forgot to divide by $1 - 1.5b = 0.78$.
Applied no maturity adjustment, as is correct for retail. A 4-year corporate loan can be downgraded, so capital is scaled up.

takeaway: For a 4-year corporate loan, capital is about 56% higher than the one-year figure because of the maturity adjustment.

setup: Two-way CSA. The portfolio is worth +USD 58.6m to the bank. The counterparty has just been downgraded from AA (threshold USD 50m) to AA- (threshold USD 25m). The bank's own threshold term is zero because the portfolio is in its favour. The bank already holds USD 8.0m of cash collateral.
ask: The credit support amount, before the minimum transfer amount and rounding, is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.6m
options.why: Still used the old AA threshold of USD 50m: $58.6 - 50 - 8.0 = 0.6$.

options.label: ≈ USD 33.6m
options.why: Subtracted the new threshold but forgot the USD 8.0m already held.

takeaway: Thresholds are rating-linked: a downgrade lowers the threshold and the call jumps. Always net off collateral already held.

setup: Unilateral CVA on an uncollateralised 5-year swap, notional USD 200m, counterparty recovery 40%, no wrong-way risk. Discounted EPE (% of notional), years 1 to 5: 2.0, 3.2, 3.6, 3.0, 1.6. Counterparty cumulative PD (%): 1.5, 3.2, 5.0, 6.9, 8.9. The dealer's own spread is 90 bp.
ask: The size of the UCVA charge is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.0014m
options.why: Left out the USD 200m notional, so the answer stays a fraction of notional (0.143%).

options.label: ≈ USD 0.79m
options.why: Weighted EPE by CUMULATIVE PDs instead of the marginal PD of each year.

options.label: ≈ USD 2.9m
options.why: Converted the percentage products with $10^{-3}$ instead of $10^{-4}$, a 10× decimal slip.

takeaway: UCVA = −LGD × Σ EPE × marginal PD × notional. The dealer's own spread belongs to DVA, not UCVA.

setup: Uncollateralised 5-year swap, notional EUR 150m, both LGDs 60%, survival adjustments ignored. $\sum EPE \times PD_C = 23.82 \times 10^{-4}$ and $\sum ENE \times PD_P = -7.66 \times 10^{-4}$ (ENE is negative). Convention: CVA negative, DVA positive, $BCVA = CVA + DVA$.
ask: Compared with the CVA leg alone, the BCVA is:

options.label: Negative, and larger in size
options.why: Subtracted the DVA from the CVA ($-0.214 - 0.069 = -0.283$). DVA is a gain, so it is added with a positive sign.

options.label: Positive
options.why: The DVA leg (0.069) is only about a third of the CVA leg (0.214), so the net cannot turn positive.

takeaway: DVA offsets part of CVA but rarely all of it. Check the sign of ENE before multiplying: a negative ENE turns the DVA into a positive number.

setup: Gregory's average-exposure approximation: $UCVA \approx -\overline{EPE} \times s_C$, as a running spread. Undiscounted EPE (% of notional), years 1 to 5: 1.8, 2.6, 3.0, 2.8, 1.8. Counterparty 5-year spread 180 bp. LGD is 60%, but it is already inside the quoted spread.
ask: The UCVA as a running spread is closest to:

options.label: ≈ -2.6 bp p.a.
options.why: Applied the 60% LGD on top of a spread that already embeds it.

options.label: ≈ -430 bp p.a.
options.why: Entered the average EPE as 2.4 instead of 0.024, a percent-as-decimal slip.

takeaway: Average EPE × credit spread gives CVA as a running spread. No LGD input is needed because the spread already prices it.

setup: A new 5-year swap, notional EUR 150m, is added to an existing netting set with the same counterparty. CVA figures (EUR m, negative convention): existing netting set $-1.84$; netting set including the new swap $-2.27$; new swap on its own $-0.96$.
ask: The upfront CVA to charge for the new swap is:

options.label: -EUR 0.96m
options.why: Used the standalone CVA and ignored that the swap partly offsets the existing trades.

options.label: -EUR 2.27m
options.why: Charged the whole netting set's CVA to the new trade, including the part already booked.

takeaway: Price a new trade at its incremental CVA: the netting set with it, minus the netting set without it.

setup: A two-way, zero-threshold CSA with daily margin on an 8-year netting set (uncollateralised CVA $-$EUR 4.2m, 250 business days a year). Best-case collateralised CVA is the uncollateralised CVA divided by $\sqrt{\text{maturity}/\text{MPoR}}$. With over 5,000 trades the MPoR is 20 business days, not the usual 10.
ask: The divisor $\sqrt{\text{maturity}/\text{MPoR}}$ is closest to:

options.why: Used the standard 10-day MPoR, $\sqrt{2000/10} = 14.1$. This netting set has 20 days.
Forgot the square root: $2000/20 = 100$.

takeaway: A longer MPoR weakens the benefit of margining: the best case leaves about 10% of the CVA here, and reality is worse.

setup: Final year of a 5-year CLO of 100 loans of USD 1m at Libor + 350 bp, Libor flat at 5%. Senior USD 85m at Libor + 50 bp, mezzanine USD 10m at Libor + 500 bp. By year 4, 24 loans have defaulted; 6 more default in year 5 (40% recovery, paid at once). The 70 survivors pay final interest and repay at par. A recovery account (5% interest) holds USD 16.385m after year 4 and is released at maturity.
ask: After the senior notes are paid in full (principal and final interest, USD 89.675m), the cash left for the mezzanine is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 3.5m
options.why: Left out the USD 2.4m of year-5 recoveries on the 6 new defaults.

options.label: ≈ USD 10.0m
options.why: Counted 76 survivors, ignoring the 6 year-5 defaults. That overstates both interest and principal.

takeaway: Waterfalls are paid top-down: with USD 5.9m left against USD 11.0m owed, the mezzanine loses about USD 5.1m.

setup: Credit card master trust, month-end receivables INR 48.0bn. Past due: 30-59 days 2.4bn; 60-89 days 1.5bn; 90-119 days 1.2bn; 120+ days 0.6bn. Receivables written off during the month: 0.36bn. For credit card ABS, a delinquent receivable is one more than 90 days past due.
ask: The delinquency ratio is closest to:

options.why: Divided 1.8 by 48.0 (0.0375) and wrote it as a percentage without multiplying by 100.
Used the month's write-offs, $0.36/48.0$. Write-offs are the default ratio, not delinquency.
Counted every past-due bucket from 30 days up ($5.7/48.0$) instead of only the 90-plus buckets.

takeaway: Delinquency ratio = 90+ day receivables / pool balance. It leads the default ratio, so a rise is an early warning for amortisation triggers.

setup: A credit card ABS has an early-amortisation trigger if the monthly payment rate (MPR) falls below 15.0%. MPR is the share of the pool repaid in the month, principal and interest together. This month: pool balance AUD 1,500m; principal collections 210m; finance-charge collections 27m; write-offs 6m; new receivables bought 180m.
ask: The trigger is:

options.label: Not hit: MPR is just above 15%
Hit: MPR is below 15%
options.why: Used principal collections only ($210/1500 = 14.0\%$). MPR counts interest collections as well.

takeaway: MPR = (principal + finance-charge collections) / pool balance. Write-offs and new purchases do not enter it.

setup: An RMBS collateral pool has three loan groups: CAD 60m at 4.0% (300 months left), CAD 90m at 5.2% (240 months left) and CAD 150m at 6.0% (120 months left). The simple average of the three mortgage rates is 5.07%.
ask: The pool's weighted average coupon (WAC), compared with 5.07%, is:

options.label: Below
options.why: The largest group (CAD 150m, half the pool) carries the highest rate, so the balance weights pull the average up, not down.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Treated the three groups as equal in size. WAC weights each rate by its balance.

takeaway: WAC weights by balance, not by group count. The remaining terms are irrelevant to WAC (they feed WAM).

setup: An RMBS pool, 18 months after origination. Start-of-month balance USD 820.0m, scheduled principal 1.4m, prepayments 5.2m, so $SMM = 5.2/818.6 = 0.635\%$ and $CPR = 7.36\%$. To state the speed against PSA, you need the 100% PSA benchmark CPR for this month.
ask: The 100% PSA CPR at month 18 is:

options.why: Used the 6% plateau, which applies only from month 30. At month 18 the pool is still on the seasoning ramp.
Used the ramp step of 0.2% per month without multiplying by the 18 months of seasoning.

takeaway: 100% PSA ramps 0.2% a month to 6% at month 30. Early in a pool's life that ramp, not 6%, is the denominator.

setup: A portfolio of two bonds: A is GBP 1.0m (PD 4%, recovery 70%), B is GBP 0.8m (PD 6%, recovery 60%). Their default correlation is 25%, with joint default probability 1.45%. Correlation then rises to 50%.
ask: The portfolio's expected credit loss:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Mixed up expected loss with unexpected loss. Correlation fattens the loss tail (VaR, UL) but expected loss is a sum of means.

options.label: Falls
options.why: Same mix-up in the other direction: more correlation never lowers the sum of the individual expected losses.

takeaway: Expected loss is additive and does not depend on default correlation. Correlation drives the spread of losses, not their mean.

setup: A USD 200m bond portfolio: AA bonds USD 120m (1-year PD 4%, recovery 65%) and BB bonds USD 80m (PD 6%, recovery 40%). Defaults are independent.
ask: Which bucket contributes more to the one-year expected loss?

options.label: BB, despite being the smaller holding
AA, because it is the larger holding
options.why: Looked at exposure alone. BB has 1.5× the PD and 1.7× the loss rate (60% against 35%), which outweighs AA's 1.5× larger balance.

options.label: They contribute equally
options.why: Neither bucket's EL matches: 1.68m for AA against 2.88m for BB.

takeaway: Loss rate is 1 minus recovery, and EL = EAD × PD × loss rate for each bucket. A smaller, riskier bucket can dominate.
